summary.text: A residue-class count modulo \(30030=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\), using \(\varphi(30030)=5760\), gives \(\pi(5M)\le M\) for every \(M\ge10^6\); hence induction bounds every term by the maximum of \(10^6\) and the five initial values. The resulting five-term state vectors range over a finite set, so two states repeat by pigeonhole, and determinism propagates that equality forever to give eventual periodicity.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes less than or equal to \(x\). Fix arbitrary initial values
\[
v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\in\mathbb N.
\]
(In particular, the argument applies when all five values are positive.) Define a sequence \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
a_i=v_i\quad(0\le i<5)
\]
and, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
a_{n+5}=\pi(a_n+a_{n+1}+a_{n+2}+a_{n+3}+a_{n+4}).
\]
We prove that this sequence is ultimately periodic.

The main point is first to obtain a bound, depending on the initial values but independent of \(n\), for every term of the sequence.

### 1. A uniform prime-counting estimate

We claim that
\[
\pi(5M)\le M\qquad\text{whenever }M\ge 1{,}000{,}000.
\tag{1}
\]

Set
\[
A=30030=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13.
\]
Since these six factors are pairwise coprime and \(\varphi(p)=p-1\) for a prime \(p\), multiplicativity of Euler's totient function gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(30030)
 &=\varphi(2)\varphi(3)\varphi(5)\varphi(7)\varphi(11)\varphi(13)\\
 &=1\cdot2\cdot4\cdot6\cdot10\cdot12\\
 &=5760.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

We use the following elementary residue-class count. If an interval of \(N\) consecutive integers is divided into complete blocks of length \(A\), together with at most one incomplete block, then at most
\[
\varphi(A)\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N}{A}\right\rfloor+1\right)
\tag{3}
\]
of its integers are coprime to \(A\). Indeed, in every complete block of \(A\) consecutive integers, each residue class modulo \(A\) occurs exactly once, and exactly \(\varphi(A)\) residue classes are coprime to \(A\). An incomplete block contains no more than \(\varphi(A)\) such residue classes.

Every prime \(p>30030\) is coprime to \(30030\). To see this, if a prime \(p\) were not coprime to \(30030\), then, because \(p\) is prime, \(p\) itself would divide \(30030\), and consequently \(p\le30030\), a contradiction.

Now suppose \(M\ge1{,}000{,}000\), and consider primes at most \(5M\). We bound the number of primes below \(30031\) crudely by \(30031\). All remaining primes lie in an interval beginning at \(30031\), are coprime to \(30030\), and the relevant interval has length \(5M-30030\). By (2) and (3),
\[
\pi(5M)
 \le 30031+5760\left(\left\lfloor\frac{5M-30030}{30030}\right\rfloor+1\right).
\tag{4}
\]
Because \(5M\ge30030\), subtracting one full block before taking the quotient shows that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{5M-30030}{30030}\right\rfloor+1
 =\left\lfloor\frac{5M}{30030}\right\rfloor.
\]
Put
\[
q=\left\lfloor\frac{5M}{30030}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then \(30030q\le5M\), and (4) becomes
\[
\pi(5M)\le30031+5760q.
\tag{5}
\]
We verify that the right-hand side is at most \(M\). The identities
\[
30030=30\cdot1001,
\qquad
5760=30\cdot192
\]
and the inequality \(30030q\le5M\) give
\[
1001\cdot5760q
 =192\cdot30030q
 \le960M.
\tag{6}
\]
Also, since \(M\ge1{,}000{,}000\),
\[
1001\cdot30031=30{,}061{,}031
 \le41{,}000{,}000
 \le41M.
\tag{7}
\]
Adding (6) and (7), we obtain
\[
1001(30031+5760q)\le(960+41)M=1001M.
\]
Thus \(30031+5760q\le M\), and (5) proves (1).

### 2. Every trajectory is bounded

Let
\[
V=\max\{v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}
\]
and define
\[
B=\max\{V,1{,}000{,}000\}.
\]
Thus every initial value is at most \(B\), and \(B\ge1{,}000{,}000\).

For each \(n\ge0\), form the five-term state, or window,
\[
S_n=(a_n,a_{n+1},a_{n+2},a_{n+3},a_{n+4}).
\]
We prove by induction on \(n\) that every coordinate of \(S_n\) is at most \(B\).

For \(n=0\), this follows directly from the definition of \(V\) and \(B\): the coordinates are \(v_0,\ldots,v_4\).

Suppose every coordinate of \(S_n\) is at most \(B\). The first four coordinates of the next state \(S_{n+1}\) are
\[
a_{n+1},a_{n+2},a_{n+3},a_{n+4},
\]
which are already coordinates of \(S_n\), so they remain at most \(B\). Its fifth coordinate is
\[
a_{n+5}=\pi(a_n+a_{n+1}+a_{n+2}+a_{n+3}+a_{n+4}).
\]
The sum inside \(\pi\) is at most \(5B\). The prime-counting function is monotone, since enlarging an interval cannot decrease the number of primes it contains. Therefore, using (1),
\[
a_{n+5}
 \le\pi(5B)
 \le B.
\]
This completes the induction. Hence
\[
a_n\le B\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0.
\tag{8}
\]
More particularly, every state \(S_n\) belongs to the finite set
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,B\}^5.
\tag{9}
\]

### 3. A state must repeat

There are infinitely many states \(S_0,S_1,S_2,\ldots\), but the set (9) contains only \((B+1)^5\) elements. By the pigeonhole principle, there exist integers \(i<j\) such that
\[
S_i=S_j.
\tag{10}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
a_{i+r}=a_{j+r}\qquad(0\le r<5).
\tag{11}
\]

### 4. Equality of states propagates forever

The recurrence is deterministic: the next state is uniquely determined by the current state. We spell this out because it is what turns a single repetition into periodicity.

Suppose, for some \(N,M\), that \(S_N=S_M\). The first four coordinates of \(S_{N+1}\) and \(S_{M+1}\) agree because they are respectively coordinates \(1,2,3,4\) of \(S_N\) and \(S_M\). For the fifth coordinates, equality of all five coordinates of the old states gives equality of their sums, and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{N+5}
 &=\pi(a_N+a_{N+1}+a_{N+2}+a_{N+3}+a_{N+4})\\
 &=\pi(a_M+a_{M+1}+a_{M+2}+a_{M+3}+a_{M+4})\\
 &=a_{M+5}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
S_N=S_M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S_{N+1}=S_{M+1}.
\tag{12}
\]
Inducting on \(k\) in (12) yields
\[
S_{N+k}=S_{M+k}\qquad\text{for every }k\ge0
\tag{13}
\]
whenever \(S_N=S_M\).

Apply (13) to the repeated states in (10). Define
\[
P=j-i.
\]
Because \(i<j\), we have \(P>0\). If \(n\ge i\), write \(n=i+k\), where \(k=n-i\ge0\). Equation (13) gives
\[
S_{i+k}=S_{j+k}.
\]
Taking the first coordinate of these states gives
\[
a_{i+k}=a_{j+k}.
\]
Since \(j=i+P\), this is precisely
\[
a_n=a_{n+P}.
\]
Thus
\[
\forall n\ge i,\qquad a_{n+P}=a_n,
\]
with \(P>0\). Taking \(N=i\) proves that the sequence is ultimately periodic.

The proof did not use positivity of the initial values; it actually establishes the stronger statement for every five initial values in \(\mathbb N\), and therefore in particular for every choice of five positive initial values.
